title: Generics and Type Hints
oneLiner: Writing code for any type without losing type checking: generic methods and classes, constraints and bounds, nullable and optional values, and Python's type hints, which a type checker reads but Python ignores at run time.
keyTakeaway: A type parameter T lets one function or class work for any type while the compiler still checks every use. Constraints (where T : IComparable<T>) say what T must support. Python's hints, list[T], int | None, look similar but are only checked by tools like mypy or Pyright, never when the program runs.
explanation:
You've used generic types since the basics: List<int> and Dictionary<string, int> are the generic List<T> and Dictionary<TKey, TValue> with their type parameters filled in. This lesson shows how to write your own generics in both languages, and how Python's optional types fit in.

C# checks types when it compiles, so a function that should work for ints, strings and anything else needs a placeholder for the type, a type parameter, usually called T. The compiler works out T from each call and checks it there. A constraint limits T to types that can do something, such as be compared, so the code inside can rely on it.

Python never needed generics to run: any function accepts anything. What it has instead are type hints, annotations such as items: list[str] -> int | None that describe the intended types. Python ignores them when running; a static type checker (mypy, Pyright, or the one in your editor) reads them and points out mistakes before you run anything. Python 3.12 added a compact syntax for type parameters, def first[T](...), and the lesson shows the older TypeVar spelling too.

Values that might be missing get the same treatment: int? in C# is a real type the compiler makes you check, and int | None in Python is a hint.
